summary: Discusses some unusual interface problems in connecting an Illinois plasma terminal, the Plato terminal, to the ARPANET.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 600 describes an interface that let a PLATO plasma terminal communicate through the ARPANET in two modes. ASCII mode supported ordinary network data, while PLATO mode carried data for the PLATO system.

questions: how to connect special terminals to networks
how did rfc 600 connect a plato terminal to the arpanet
what was ascii mode used for
subtitle: An interface design for connecting a PLATO plasma terminal to the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The PLATO IV plasma terminal used a nonstandard communication scheme, making it difficult to connect through the ARPANET and use for other applications.
tldr.mechanism: The prototype interface offered an ASCII mode for network-oriented data and a PLATO mode for passing PLATO data in 8-bit codes through the network.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a prototype in use at UCSB and plans to repackage the hardware around a programmable microcomputer.

today: RFC 600 documents a UCSB prototype interface for connecting a PLATO plasma terminal to the ARPANET.

sections.title: Why the Terminal Needed an Interface
sections.content:
The PLATO IV system at the University of Illinois used a plasma display terminal with a communication scheme based on frequency-shift keying. The RFC says long-distance telephone use cost money and the scheme was nonstandard, limiting use of the terminal in other applications. An ARPANET connection near PLATO offered another way to link the terminal to computer resources.

To connect through a TIP, the terminal needed to communicate using Teletype-like codes. Reaching PLATO through the network without changing PLATO itself also required an interface that could use its FSK communication scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The PLATO terminal used a communication method that did not match the ARPANET's ordinary terminal interface. A special interface was needed to support both network access and communication with PLATO.

sections.title: ASCII and PLATO Modes
sections.content:
The interface was designed to operate in two modes. ASCII mode sent and received 8-bit ASCII for network-oriented use, such as logging in through a TIP; it had no graphics capability, and the keyboard could send 124 codes. PLATO mode embedded PLATO data in 8-bit codes so it could pass transparently through the network. The interface could also use an ASCII keyboard while keeping the display in PLATO mode.

In PLATO mode, some code values could be mistaken for network commands. The RFC gives @ as a TIP command prefix and says the interface had to double such a code or omit it.
sections.plainLanguage: ASCII mode let the terminal handle ordinary network input but did not provide graphics. PLATO mode carried PLATO data, with special handling to prevent a code from being mistaken for a network command.

sections.title: Planned Interface Development
sections.content:
The prototype was in use at UCSB. After discussion, the developers decided to repackage the original hardware using a microcomputer with a ROM control program. They expected added RAM or ROM to make it possible to program a wider range of tasks, including emulating standard graphics terminals, implementing a cursor and responding to Network Graphics Protocols. The RFC says development of this interface had begun at UCSB.

The document also includes a planned data-packing figure and notes that the PLATO System hardware removes NO-OP codes from the data stream at its end.
sections.plainLanguage: UCSB planned a programmable microcomputer-based interface to make the terminal more flexible. The proposed work included graphics-terminal emulation and support for network graphics protocols.
